questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: A current carrying circular loop of radius 2 cm with unit normal $\hat{n}=\frac{\hat{k}+\hat{i}}{\sqrt{2}}$ is placed in a magnetic field, $\vec{B}=B_{o}(3\hat{i}+2\hat{k})$ . If $B_{o}=4 \times 10^{-3}T$ and current $I=100\sqrt{2}A$ , the torque experienced by the loop is $____$ Wb.A. ( $\pi=3.14$ )
questions.question_html: A current carrying circular loop of radius 2 cm with unit normal $\hat{n}=\frac{\hat{k}+\hat{i}}{\sqrt{2}}$ is placed in a magnetic field, $\vec{B}=B_{o}(3\hat{i}+2\hat{k})$ . If $B_{o}=4 \times 10^{-3}T$ and current $I=100\sqrt{2}A$ , the torque experienced by the loop is $____$ Wb.A. ( $\pi=3.14$ )
questions.explanation_text: When a current-carrying loop is placed in an external magnetic field, it experiences a torque $(\vec{\tau})$ . The magnetic properties of the loop are represented by its magnetic dipole moment $(\vec{m})$ , defined as : $\vec{m}=I\vec{A}$ Where I is the current and $\vec{A}$ is the area vector of the loop. The direction of the area vector is perpendicular to the plane of the loop, given by the unit normal $\hat{n}$ . $\vec{A}=A\hat{n}$ The torque is given by the cross product of the magnetic moment and the magnetic field : $\vec{\tau}=\vec{m} \times \vec{B}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{\tau}=(IA\hat{n}) \times \vec{B}$ The radius of circular loop is $r=2cm=0.02m$ . So, the area is $A=\pi r^{2}=\pi(0.02)^{2}=4\pi \times 10^{-4}m^{2}$ The unit normal is $\hat{n}=\frac{\hat{k}+\hat{t}}{\sqrt{2}}$ And the current in loop is $I=100\sqrt{2}A$ So, the magnetic moment vector is; $\vec{m}=(100\sqrt{2}) \times (4\pi \times 10^{-4}) \times (\frac{\hat{ı}+\hat{k}}{\sqrt{2}})$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{m}=400\pi \times 10^{-4}(\hat{ı}+\hat{k})=0.04\pi(\hat{ı}+\hat{k})A \cdot m^{2}$ The magnetic field in the region is $\vec{B}=B_{o}(3\hat{ı}+2\hat{k})$ with $B_{o}=4 \times 10^{-3}T$ $\vec{B}=4 \times 10^{-3}(3\hat{ı}+2\hat{k})=(12\hat{ı}+8\hat{k}) \times 10^{-3}T$ Using the formula for magnetic torque, $\vec{\tau}=\vec{m} \times \vec{B}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{\tau}=[0.04\pi(\hat{ı}+\hat{k})] \times [(12\hat{ı}+8\hat{k}) \times 10^{-3}]$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{\tau}=(0.04\pi \times 10^{-3})[(\hat{ı}+\hat{k}) \times (12\hat{ı}+8\hat{k})]$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{\tau}=(0.04\pi \times 10^{-3})(4\hat{ȷ})$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{\tau}=0.16\pi \times 10^{-3}\hat{ȷ}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{\tau}=0.16 \times 3.14 \times 10^{-3}\hat{ȷ}=0.5024 \times 10^{-3}\hat{ȷ}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{\tau}=5024 \times 10^{-7}\hat{ȷ}$ Therefore, the torque experienced by the loop is $5024 \times 10^{-7}\hat{j}$ . Hence, the correct option is (D).
questions.explanation_html:
When a current-carrying loop is placed in an external magnetic field, it experiences a torque $(\vec{\tau})$ . The magnetic properties of the loop are represented by its magnetic dipole moment $(\vec{m})$ , defined as :

$\vec{m}=I\vec{A}$

Where I is the current and $\vec{A}$ is the area vector of the loop. The direction of the area vector is perpendicular to the plane of the loop, given by the unit normal $\hat{n}$ .

$\vec{A}=A\hat{n}$

The torque is given by the cross product of the magnetic moment and the magnetic field :

$\vec{\tau}=\vec{m} \times \vec{B}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\vec{\tau}=(IA\hat{n}) \times \vec{B}$

The radius of circular loop is $r=2cm=0.02m$ .

So, the area is

$A=\pi r^{2}=\pi(0.02)^{2}=4\pi \times 10^{-4}m^{2}$

The unit normal is $\hat{n}=\frac{\hat{k}+\hat{t}}{\sqrt{2}}$

And the current in loop is $I=100\sqrt{2}A$

So, the magnetic moment vector is;

$\vec{m}=(100\sqrt{2}) \times (4\pi \times 10^{-4}) \times (\frac{\hat{ı}+\hat{k}}{\sqrt{2}})$

$\Rightarrow$ $\vec{m}=400\pi \times 10^{-4}(\hat{ı}+\hat{k})=0.04\pi(\hat{ı}+\hat{k})A \cdot m^{2}$

The magnetic field in the region is $\vec{B}=B_{o}(3\hat{ı}+2\hat{k})$ with $B_{o}=4 \times 10^{-3}T$

$\vec{B}=4 \times 10^{-3}(3\hat{ı}+2\hat{k})=(12\hat{ı}+8\hat{k}) \times 10^{-3}T$

Using the formula for magnetic torque,

$\vec{\tau}=\vec{m} \times \vec{B}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\vec{\tau}=[0.04\pi(\hat{ı}+\hat{k})] \times [(12\hat{ı}+8\hat{k}) \times 10^{-3}]$

$\Rightarrow$ $\vec{\tau}=(0.04\pi \times 10^{-3})[(\hat{ı}+\hat{k}) \times (12\hat{ı}+8\hat{k})]$

$\Rightarrow$ $\vec{\tau}=(0.04\pi \times 10^{-3})(4\hat{ȷ})$

$\Rightarrow$ $\vec{\tau}=0.16\pi \times 10^{-3}\hat{ȷ}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\vec{\tau}=0.16 \times 3.14 \times 10^{-3}\hat{ȷ}=0.5024 \times 10^{-3}\hat{ȷ}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\vec{\tau}=5024 \times 10^{-7}\hat{ȷ}$

Therefore, the torque experienced by the loop is $5024 \times 10^{-7}\hat{j}$ .

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.question_text: An insulated wire is wound so that it forms a flat coil with $N=200$ turns. The radius of the innermost turn is $r_{1}=3cm$ , and of the outermost turn $r_{2}=6cm$ . If 20 mA current flows in it then the magnetic moment will be $\alpha \times 10^{-2}A.m^{2}$ . The value of $\alpha$ is $____$ .
questions.question_html: An insulated wire is wound so that it forms a flat coil with $N=200$ turns. The radius of the innermost turn is $r_{1}=3cm$ , and of the outermost turn $r_{2}=6cm$ . If 20 mA current flows in it then the magnetic moment will be $\alpha \times 10^{-2}A.m^{2}$ . The value of $\alpha$ is $____$ .
questions.explanation_text: For a single circular turn of radius $r$ carrying current $I$ , the magnetic moment is : $m=I \cdot A=I(\pi r^{2})$ In a flat coil where the turns are wound from $r_{1}$ to $r_{2}$ , the number of turns per unit radial length is $n=\frac{N}{r_{2}-r_{1}}$ . The total magnetic moment ( M ) is the integral of the moments of all infinitesimal turns of thickness dr : $M=\int_{r_{1}}^{r_{2}}(I\pi r^{2}) \cdot ndr$ $\Rightarrow$ $M=I\pi n\int_{r_{1}}^{r_{2}}r^{2}dr=I\pi(\frac{N}{r_{2}-r_{1}})[\frac{r^{3}}{3}]_{r_{1}}^{r_{2}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $M=\frac{NI\pi}{3(r_{2}-r_{1})}(r_{2}^{3}-r_{1}^{3})$ Using the algebraic identity $r_{2}^{3}-r_{1}^{3}=(r_{2}-r_{1})(r_{2}^{2}+r_{1}^{2}+r_{1}r_{2})$ : $M=\frac{NI\pi}{3}(r_{1}^{2}+r_{2}^{2}+r_{1}r_{2})$ Substituting the values, where number of turns is $N=200$ , the current is $I=20mA=20 \times 10^{-3}A$ , the inner radius of coil is $r_{1}=3cm=0.03m$ and the outer radius is $r_{2}=6cm=0.06m$ $M=\frac{200 \times 20 \times 10^{-3} \times 3.14}{3}(0.03^{2}+0.06^{2}+0.03 \times 0.06)$ $\Rightarrow$ $M=\frac{4 \times 3.14}{3}(0.0009+0.0036+0.0018)$ $\Rightarrow$ $M=\frac{12.56}{3}(0.0063)=12.56 \times 0.0021$ $\Rightarrow$ $M=0.026376 \approx 2.64 \times 10^{-2}A.m^{2}=\alpha \times 10^{-2}A.m^{2} \Rightarrow \alpha=2.64$ Therefore, the value of $\alpha$ is 2.64 . Thus, the correct option is (B).
questions.explanation_html:
For a single circular turn of radius $r$ carrying current $I$ , the magnetic moment is :

$m=I \cdot A=I(\pi r^{2})$

In a flat coil where the turns are wound from $r_{1}$ to $r_{2}$ , the number of turns per unit radial length is $n=\frac{N}{r_{2}-r_{1}}$ . The total magnetic moment ( M ) is the integral of the moments of all infinitesimal turns of thickness dr :

$M=\int_{r_{1}}^{r_{2}}(I\pi r^{2}) \cdot ndr$

$\Rightarrow$ $M=I\pi n\int_{r_{1}}^{r_{2}}r^{2}dr=I\pi(\frac{N}{r_{2}-r_{1}})[\frac{r^{3}}{3}]_{r_{1}}^{r_{2}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $M=\frac{NI\pi}{3(r_{2}-r_{1})}(r_{2}^{3}-r_{1}^{3})$

Using the algebraic identity $r_{2}^{3}-r_{1}^{3}=(r_{2}-r_{1})(r_{2}^{2}+r_{1}^{2}+r_{1}r_{2})$ :

$M=\frac{NI\pi}{3}(r_{1}^{2}+r_{2}^{2}+r_{1}r_{2})$

Substituting the values, where number of turns is $N=200$ , the current is $I=20mA=20 \times 10^{-3}A$ , the inner radius of coil is $r_{1}=3cm=0.03m$ and the outer radius is $r_{2}=6cm=0.06m$

$M=\frac{200 \times 20 \times 10^{-3} \times 3.14}{3}(0.03^{2}+0.06^{2}+0.03 \times 0.06)$

$\Rightarrow$ $M=\frac{4 \times 3.14}{3}(0.0009+0.0036+0.0018)$

$\Rightarrow$ $M=\frac{12.56}{3}(0.0063)=12.56 \times 0.0021$

$\Rightarrow$ $M=0.026376 \approx 2.64 \times 10^{-2}A.m^{2}=\alpha \times 10^{-2}A.m^{2} \Rightarrow \alpha=2.64$

Therefore, the value of $\alpha$ is 2.64 .

Thus, the correct option is (B).

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: The magnetic field at the centre of a current carrying circular loop of radius $R$ is $16\mu T$ . The magnetic field at a distance $x=\sqrt{3}R$ on its axis from the centre is $____$ $\mu T$ .
questions.question_html:
The magnetic field at the centre of a current carrying circular loop of radius $R$ is $16\mu T$ . The magnetic field at a distance $x=\sqrt{3}R$ on its axis from the centre is

$____$ $\mu T$ .
questions.explanation_text: The magnetic field at the centre of a circular loop of radius R carrying current i is given by: $B_{c}=\frac{\mu_{0}i}{2R}$ We are given that $B_{c}=16\mu T$ . The magnetic field at a point on the axis at a distance x from the centre is given by: $B_{a}=\frac{\mu_{0}iR^{2}}{2(R^{2}+x^{2})^{\frac{3}{2}}}$ The ratio of magnetic field at the centre to the axis, $\frac{B_{C}}{B_{a}}=\frac{(\frac{\mu_{0}i}{2R})}{⎛⎝⎜\frac{\mu_{0}iR^{2}}{2(R^{2}+x^{2})^{\frac{3}{2}}}⎞⎠⎟}$ $\Rightarrow B_{a}=B_{c}[\frac{R^{3}}{(R^{2}+x^{2})^{3/2}}]$ Given the distance $x=\sqrt{3}R$ , $\Rightarrow B_{a}=B_{c}[\frac{R^{3}}{(R^{2}+(\sqrt{3}R)^{2})^{3/2}}]=\frac{B_{c}}{8}$ $\Rightarrow$ $B_{a}=\frac{16\mu T}{8}=2\mu T$ Hence, the correct option is (B).
questions.explanation_html:
The magnetic field at the centre of a circular loop of radius R carrying current i is given by:

$B_{c}=\frac{\mu_{0}i}{2R}$

We are given that $B_{c}=16\mu T$ .

The magnetic field at a point on the axis at a distance x from the centre is given by:

$B_{a}=\frac{\mu_{0}iR^{2}}{2(R^{2}+x^{2})^{\frac{3}{2}}}$

The ratio of magnetic field at the centre to the axis,

$\frac{B_{C}}{B_{a}}=\frac{(\frac{\mu_{0}i}{2R})}{⎛⎝⎜\frac{\mu_{0}iR^{2}}{2(R^{2}+x^{2})^{\frac{3}{2}}}⎞⎠⎟}$

$\Rightarrow B_{a}=B_{c}[\frac{R^{3}}{(R^{2}+x^{2})^{3/2}}]$

Given the distance $x=\sqrt{3}R$ ,

$\Rightarrow B_{a}=B_{c}[\frac{R^{3}}{(R^{2}+(\sqrt{3}R)^{2})^{3/2}}]=\frac{B_{c}}{8}$

$\Rightarrow$ $B_{a}=\frac{16\mu T}{8}=2\mu T$

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.question_text: An infinitely long straight wire carrying current $I$ is bent in a planar shape as shown in the diagram. The radius of the circular part is $r$ . The magnetic field at the centre $O$ of the circular loop is :
questions.question_html: An infinitely long straight wire carrying current $I$ is bent in a planar shape as shown in the diagram. The radius of the circular part is $r$ . The magnetic field at the centre $O$ of the circular loop is :
questions.explanation_text: The segments AB and DE together form an infinitely long straight wire. For an infinite wire the magnitude of the magnetic field at distance r is given as $B_{\text{straight}}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r}$ Using the Right-Hand Thumb Rule, if the thumb points in the direction of current I (along +y ), the fingers curl out of the page at point O , i.e., in the -x direction. $\vec{B}_{\text{straight}}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r}\hat{ı}$ The circular part is a nearly complete loop of radius r . For a circular loop at its centre the magnitude of the magnetic field is given as, $B_{\text{loop}}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2r}$ Using the Right-Hand Rule for loops, curling the fingers in the direction of the current (clockwise in the yz -plane) the thumb points into the page, which is the -x direction. $\vec{B}_{loop}=-\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2r}\hat{i}$ The total field is the vector sum of both parts : $\vec{B}_{\text{total}}=\vec{B}_{\text{straight}}+\vec{B}_{loop}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{B}_{total}=(\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r})\hat{i}+(-\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2r})\hat{i}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{B}_{\text{total}}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2r}[\frac{1}{\pi}-1]\hat{i}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r}[1-\pi]\hat{i}=-\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r}[\pi-1]\hat{i}$ So, the magnetic field at the centre O of the circular loop is $=-\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r}[\pi-1]\hat{1}$ . Hence, the correct option is (B).
questions.explanation_html:
The segments AB and DE together form an infinitely long straight wire.

For an infinite wire the magnitude of the magnetic field at distance r is given as

$B_{\text{straight}}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r}$

Using the Right-Hand Thumb Rule, if the thumb points in the direction of current I (along +y ), the fingers curl out of the page at point O , i.e., in the -x direction.

$\vec{B}_{\text{straight}}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r}\hat{ı}$

The circular part is a nearly complete loop of radius r .

For a circular loop at its centre the magnitude of the magnetic field is given as,

$B_{\text{loop}}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2r}$

Using the Right-Hand Rule for loops, curling the fingers in the direction of the current (clockwise in the yz -plane) the thumb points into the page, which is the -x direction.

$\vec{B}_{loop}=-\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2r}\hat{i}$

The total field is the vector sum of both parts :

$\vec{B}_{\text{total}}=\vec{B}_{\text{straight}}+\vec{B}_{loop}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\vec{B}_{total}=(\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r})\hat{i}+(-\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2r})\hat{i}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\vec{B}_{\text{total}}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2r}[\frac{1}{\pi}-1]\hat{i}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r}[1-\pi]\hat{i}=-\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r}[\pi-1]\hat{i}$

So, the magnetic field at the centre O of the circular loop is $=-\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r}[\pi-1]\hat{1}$ .

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: A circular coil of radius 2 cm and 125 turns carries a current of 1 A . The coil is placed in a uniform magnetic field of magnitude 0.4 T . The axis of the coil makes an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the direction of the magnetic field. The torque acting on the coil is $\alpha \times 10^{-4}N.m$ . The value of $\alpha$ is $____$ . $(\pi=3.14)$
questions.question_html:
A circular coil of radius 2 cm and 125 turns carries a current of 1 A . The coil is placed in a uniform magnetic field of magnitude 0.4 T . The axis of the coil makes an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the direction of the magnetic field. The torque acting on the coil is $\alpha \times 10^{-4}N.m$ . The value of $\alpha$ is $____$ .

$(\pi=3.14)$
questions.explanation_text: The magnetic dipole moment of a single loop of wire carrying current I and enclosing area A is given by $m=IA$ For a coil consisting of N turns, the total magnetic moment is : $m=NIA$ Since the coil is circular with radius r , the area A is $\pi r^{2}$ . $m=NI(\pi r^{2})$ The torque experienced by a magnetic dipole in a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is given by the vector cross product : $\vec{\tau}=\vec{m} \times \vec{B}$ The magnitude of this torque is : $\tau=mBsin\theta$ Where $\theta$ is the angle between the magnetic moment (which is along the axis of the coil) and the magnetic field direction. The number of turns is $N=125$ . The current in the coil is $I=1A$ . The radius of circular coil is $r=2cm=0.02m$ . The magnitude of magnetic field strength is, $B=0.4T$ . The angle between the magnetic field and magnetic moment is $\theta=30^{\circ}$ . Substituting the values into the torque formula: $\tau=(NI\pi r^{2})Bsin\theta$ $\Rightarrow$ $\tau=(125 \times 1 \times 3.14 \times (0.02)^{2}) \times 0.4 \times sin30^{\circ}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\tau=(125 \times 3.14 \times 0.0004) \times 0.4 \times 0.5$ $\Rightarrow$ $\tau=314 \times 10^{-4}N.m=\alpha \times 10^{-4}N \cdot m \Rightarrow \alpha=314$ Therefore, the value of a is 314 .
questions.explanation_html:
The magnetic dipole moment of a single loop of wire carrying current I and enclosing area A is given by

$m=IA$

For a coil consisting of N turns, the total magnetic moment is :

$m=NIA$

Since the coil is circular with radius r , the area A is $\pi r^{2}$ .

$m=NI(\pi r^{2})$

The torque experienced by a magnetic dipole in a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is given by the vector cross product :

$\vec{\tau}=\vec{m} \times \vec{B}$

The magnitude of this torque is :

$\tau=mBsin\theta$

Where $\theta$ is the angle between the magnetic moment (which is along the axis of the coil) and the magnetic field direction.

The number of turns is $N=125$ .

The current in the coil is $I=1A$ .

The radius of circular coil is $r=2cm=0.02m$ .

The magnitude of magnetic field strength is, $B=0.4T$ .

The angle between the magnetic field and magnetic moment is $\theta=30^{\circ}$ .

Substituting the values into the torque formula:

$\tau=(NI\pi r^{2})Bsin\theta$

$\Rightarrow$ $\tau=(125 \times 1 \times 3.14 \times (0.02)^{2}) \times 0.4 \times sin30^{\circ}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\tau=(125 \times 3.14 \times 0.0004) \times 0.4 \times 0.5$

$\Rightarrow$ $\tau=314 \times 10^{-4}N.m=\alpha \times 10^{-4}N \cdot m \Rightarrow \alpha=314$

Therefore, the value of a is 314 .

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: A current of 30 A each flows in opposite directions in two conducting wires, placed parallel to each other at a distance of 8 cm . The magnetic field at the mid point between the two wires is $____$ $\mu T$ . $(\frac{\mu_{o}}{4\pi}=10^{-7}N/A^{2})$
questions.question_html:
A current of 30 A each flows in opposite directions in two conducting wires, placed parallel to each other at a distance of 8 cm . The magnetic field at the mid point between the two wires is $____$ $\mu T$ .

$(\frac{\mu_{o}}{4\pi}=10^{-7}N/A^{2})$
questions.explanation_text: According to the Ampere's circuital Law, the magnetic field B at a distance r from an infinitely long straight wire carrying current I is : $∮\vec{B} \cdot d\vec{l}=\mu_{0}I$ For a circular path of radius $r$ : $B(2\pi r)=\mu_{0}I \Rightarrow B=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r}$ Let the wires be $W_{1}$ and $W_{2}$ separated by $d=8cm$ . The midpoint is at $r=4cm=0.04m$ from each wire. Wire 1 carries current along out of the page. Using the right-hand rule, the field $B_{1}$ at the midpoint points along $y$ -axis. Wire 2 carries current along into the page. Using the right-hand rule, the field $B_{2}$ at the midpoint also points along y -axis. Since both fields point in the same direction, the net magnetic field $B_{\text{net}}=B_{1}+B_{2}$ . The current in the wires are given as $I_{1}=I_{2}=30A$ and $r=0.04m$ : $B_{1}=B_{2}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r}=2 \times (\frac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi})\frac{I}{r}$ $\Rightarrow$ $B_{1}=B_{2}=2 \times 10^{-7} \times \frac{30}{0.04}=2 \times 10^{-7} \times 750=15 \times 10^{-5}T$ $\Rightarrow$ $B_{\text{net}}=15 \times 10^{-5}+15 \times 10^{-5}=30 \times 10^{-5}T$ $\Rightarrow$ $B_{net}=300 \times 10^{-6}T=300\mu T$ Therefore, the magnitude of magnetic field at the midpoint is $300\mu T$ . Thus, the correct option is (B).
questions.explanation_html:
According to the Ampere's circuital Law, the magnetic field B at a distance r from an infinitely long straight wire carrying current I is :

$∮\vec{B} \cdot d\vec{l}=\mu_{0}I$

For a circular path of radius $r$ :

$B(2\pi r)=\mu_{0}I \Rightarrow B=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r}$

Let the wires be $W_{1}$ and $W_{2}$ separated by $d=8cm$ . The midpoint is at $r=4cm=0.04m$ from each wire.

Wire 1 carries current along out of the page. Using the right-hand rule, the field $B_{1}$ at the midpoint points along $y$ -axis.

Wire 2 carries current along into the page. Using the right-hand rule, the field $B_{2}$ at the midpoint also points along y -axis.

Since both fields point in the same direction, the net magnetic field $B_{\text{net}}=B_{1}+B_{2}$ .

The current in the wires are given as $I_{1}=I_{2}=30A$ and $r=0.04m$ :

$B_{1}=B_{2}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r}=2 \times (\frac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi})\frac{I}{r}$

$\Rightarrow$ $B_{1}=B_{2}=2 \times 10^{-7} \times \frac{30}{0.04}=2 \times 10^{-7} \times 750=15 \times 10^{-5}T$

$\Rightarrow$ $B_{\text{net}}=15 \times 10^{-5}+15 \times 10^{-5}=30 \times 10^{-5}T$

$\Rightarrow$ $B_{net}=300 \times 10^{-6}T=300\mu T$

Therefore, the magnitude of magnetic field at the midpoint is $300\mu T$ .

Thus, the correct option is (B).

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: A particle having charge $10^{-9}$ C moving in $x$ - $y$ plane in fields of $0.4\hat{j}$ N/C and $4 \times 10^{-3}\hat{k}$ T experiences a force of $(4\hat{i}+2\hat{j}) \times 10^{-10}$ N. The velocity of the particle at that instant is _________ m/s.
questions.question_html: A particle having charge $10^{-9}$ C moving in $x$ - $y$ plane in fields of $0.4\hat{j}$ N/C and $4 \times 10^{-3}\hat{k}$ T experiences a force of $(4\hat{i}+2\hat{j}) \times 10^{-10}$ N. The velocity of the particle at that instant is _________ m/s.
questions.explanation_text: The total force on the charged particle is found by adding the electric force and the magnetic force: $\vec{F}=q\vec{E}+q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$ Here, the charge on the particle is $q=10^{-9}C$ . The force acting on it is $\vec{F}=(4\hat{i}+2\hat{j}) \times 10^{-10}N$ . The electric field is $\vec{E}=0.4\hat{j}N/C$ . The magnetic field is $\vec{B}=4 \times 10^{-3}\hat{k}T$ . Since the particle is moving in the $x$ - $y$ plane, let its velocity be $\vec{v}=v_{x}\hat{i}+v_{y}\hat{j}$ . Now, calculate the cross product: $\vec{v} \times \vec{B}=(v_{x}\hat{i}+v_{y}\hat{j}) \times (4 \times 10^{-3}\hat{k})$ Using the rules $\hat{i} \times \hat{k}=-\hat{j}$ and $\hat{j} \times \hat{k}=\hat{i}$ : $\vec{v} \times \vec{B}=4 \times 10^{-3}v_{y}\hat{i}-4 \times 10^{-3}v_{x}\hat{j}$ Substitute in the main force equation after dividing both sides by $q$ : $\frac{(4\hat{i}+2\hat{j}) \times 10^{-10}}{10^{-9}}=0.4\hat{j}+[(4 \times 10^{-3}v_{y})\hat{i}-(4 \times 10^{-3}v_{x})\hat{j}]$ This simplifies to: $0.4\hat{i}+0.2\hat{j}=(4 \times 10^{-3}v_{y})\hat{i}-(4 \times 10^{-3}v_{x}+0.4)\hat{j}$ Comparing components along $\hat{i}$ : $0.4=4 \times 10^{-3}v_{y}$ $v_{y}=\frac{0.4}{4 \times 10^{-3}}=100m/s$ Comparing components along $\hat{j}$ : $0.2=0.4-4 \times 10^{-3}v_{x}$ $4 \times 10^{-3}v_{x}=0.2$ $v_{x}=50m/s$ Hence, the velocity of the particle is: $\vec{v}=50\hat{i}+100\hat{j}m/s$ Therefore, the correct answer is (A).
questions.explanation_html:
The total force on the charged particle is found by adding the electric force and the magnetic force:

$\vec{F}=q\vec{E}+q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$

Here, the charge on the particle is $q=10^{-9}C$ .

The force acting on it is $\vec{F}=(4\hat{i}+2\hat{j}) \times 10^{-10}N$ .

The electric field is $\vec{E}=0.4\hat{j}N/C$ .

The magnetic field is $\vec{B}=4 \times 10^{-3}\hat{k}T$ .

Since the particle is moving in the $x$ - $y$ plane, let its velocity be $\vec{v}=v_{x}\hat{i}+v_{y}\hat{j}$ .

Now, calculate the cross product:

$\vec{v} \times \vec{B}=(v_{x}\hat{i}+v_{y}\hat{j}) \times (4 \times 10^{-3}\hat{k})$

Using the rules $\hat{i} \times \hat{k}=-\hat{j}$ and $\hat{j} \times \hat{k}=\hat{i}$ :

$\vec{v} \times \vec{B}=4 \times 10^{-3}v_{y}\hat{i}-4 \times 10^{-3}v_{x}\hat{j}$

Substitute in the main force equation after dividing both sides by $q$ :

$\frac{(4\hat{i}+2\hat{j}) \times 10^{-10}}{10^{-9}}=0.4\hat{j}+[(4 \times 10^{-3}v_{y})\hat{i}-(4 \times 10^{-3}v_{x})\hat{j}]$

This simplifies to:

$0.4\hat{i}+0.2\hat{j}=(4 \times 10^{-3}v_{y})\hat{i}-(4 \times 10^{-3}v_{x}+0.4)\hat{j}$

Comparing components along $\hat{i}$ :

$0.4=4 \times 10^{-3}v_{y}$

$v_{y}=\frac{0.4}{4 \times 10^{-3}}=100m/s$

Comparing components along $\hat{j}$ :

$0.2=0.4-4 \times 10^{-3}v_{x}$

$4 \times 10^{-3}v_{x}=0.2$

$v_{x}=50m/s$

Hence, the velocity of the particle is:

$\vec{v}=50\hat{i}+100\hat{j}m/s$

Therefore, the correct answer is (A).

questions.question_text: Three long straight wires carrying current are arranged mutually parallel as shown in the figure. The force experienced by 15 cm length of wire $Q$ is $____$ . $(\mu_{o}=4\pi \times 10^{-7}T.m/A)$
questions.question_html:
Three long straight wires carrying current are arranged mutually parallel as shown in the figure. The force experienced by 15 cm length of wire $Q$ is $____$ .

$(\mu_{o}=4\pi \times 10^{-7}T.m/A)$
questions.explanation_text: Using the formula for the force per unit length between two parallel current-carrying wires : $\frac{F}{l}=\frac{\mu_{0}I_{1}I_{2}}{2\pi r}$ Wires P and Q carry currents in opposite directions (3 A up and 1 A down). Parallel wires with opposite currents repel each other. Therefore, wire $P$ pushes wire $Q$ to the right (towards wire $R$ ) with a force $F_{PQ}$ Given $I_{P}=3A,I_{Q}=1A,r_{PQ}=3cm=0.03m$ So, the magnitude of force on 15 cm of wire Q due to wire P is, $F_{PQ}=\frac{(4\pi \times 10^{-7}) \times 3 \times 1 \times 0.15}{2\pi \times 0.03}N=3 \times 10^{-6}N$ Wires Q and R carry currents in the same direction ( 1 A down and 2 A down). Parallel wires with samedirection currents attract each other. Therefore, wire $R$ pulls wire $Q$ to the right (towards wire $R$ ) with force $F_{RQ}$ . Given that $I_{R}=2A,I_{Q}=1A,r_{RQ}=2cm=0.02m$ $F_{RQ}=\frac{(4\pi \times 10^{-7}) \times 2 \times 1 \times 0.15}{2\pi \times 0.02}$ $\Rightarrow$ $F_{RQ}=\frac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 0.30}{0.02}=2 \times 10^{-7} \times 15=3 \times 10^{-6}N$ Since both forces acting on wire $Q$ are directed towards the right, the net force will be towards $R$ . $F_{net}=F_{PQ}+F_{RQ}$ $\Rightarrow$ $F_{\text{net}}=3 \times 10^{-6}+3 \times 10^{-6}$ $F_{net}=6 \times 10^{-6}N$ Hence, the net force acting on wire $Q$ is $6 \times 10^{-6}N$ towards $R$ . Hence, the correct option is (B).
questions.explanation_html:
Using the formula for the force per unit length between two parallel current-carrying wires :

$\frac{F}{l}=\frac{\mu_{0}I_{1}I_{2}}{2\pi r}$

Wires P and Q carry currents in opposite directions (3 A up and 1 A down). Parallel wires with opposite currents repel each other. Therefore, wire $P$ pushes wire $Q$ to the right (towards wire $R$ ) with a force $F_{PQ}$

Given $I_{P}=3A,I_{Q}=1A,r_{PQ}=3cm=0.03m$

So, the magnitude of force on 15 cm of wire Q due to wire P is,

$F_{PQ}=\frac{(4\pi \times 10^{-7}) \times 3 \times 1 \times 0.15}{2\pi \times 0.03}N=3 \times 10^{-6}N$

Wires Q and R carry currents in the same direction ( 1 A down and 2 A down). Parallel wires with samedirection currents attract each other. Therefore, wire $R$ pulls wire $Q$ to the right (towards wire $R$ ) with force $F_{RQ}$ .

Given that $I_{R}=2A,I_{Q}=1A,r_{RQ}=2cm=0.02m$

$F_{RQ}=\frac{(4\pi \times 10^{-7}) \times 2 \times 1 \times 0.15}{2\pi \times 0.02}$

$\Rightarrow$ $F_{RQ}=\frac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 0.30}{0.02}=2 \times 10^{-7} \times 15=3 \times 10^{-6}N$

Since both forces acting on wire $Q$ are directed towards the right, the net force will be towards $R$ .

$F_{net}=F_{PQ}+F_{RQ}$

$\Rightarrow$ $F_{\text{net}}=3 \times 10^{-6}+3 \times 10^{-6}$

$F_{net}=6 \times 10^{-6}N$

Hence, the net force acting on wire $Q$ is $6 \times 10^{-6}N$ towards $R$ .

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.question_text: A current carrying solenoid is placed vertically and a particle of mass $m$ with charge $Q$ is released from rest. The particle moves along the axis of solenoid. If $g$ is acceleration due to gravity then the acceleration (a) of the charged particle will satisfy :
questions.question_html: A current carrying solenoid is placed vertically and a particle of mass $m$ with charge $Q$ is released from rest. The particle moves along the axis of solenoid. If $g$ is acceleration due to gravity then the acceleration (a) of the charged particle will satisfy :
questions.explanation_text: A current-carrying solenoid produces a magnetic field ( $\vec{B}$ ). For an ideal solenoid, the magnetic field inside is uniform and directed parallel to its axis. The magnetic force $(\vec{F}_{m})$ on a moving charge $Q$ with velocity $\vec{v}$ is given by the Lorentz force formula : $\vec{F}_{m}=Q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$ In this case, the charged particle is released from rest along the axis. The magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is also along the axis. Therefore, the velocity $\vec{v}$ (once the particle starts moving) and the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ are parallel to each other. The magnitude of the magnetic force is the cross product of $Q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$ , $F_{m}=QvBsin\theta$ Since the angle $\theta$ between the velocity and the magnetic field is $0^{\circ}$ : $F_{m}=QvBsin0^{\circ}$ The magnetic field exerts no force on the particle moving along the axis. The solenoid is placed vertically. When the particle of mass $m$ is released, the only non-zero force acting on it is the force of gravity $(\vec{F}_{g})$ : $\vec{F}_{g}=mg$ This force acts vertically downwards along the axis of the solenoid. According to Newton's Second Law ( $F_{\text{net}}=ma$ ) : $mg=ma$ $\Rightarrow a=g$ Since the magnetic force is zero the particle falls freely under gravity. Thus, its acceleration is exactly equal to g. Hence, the correct option is (D).
questions.explanation_html:
A current-carrying solenoid produces a magnetic field ( $\vec{B}$ ). For an ideal solenoid, the magnetic field inside is uniform and directed parallel to its axis.

The magnetic force $(\vec{F}_{m})$ on a moving charge $Q$ with velocity $\vec{v}$ is given by the Lorentz force formula :

$\vec{F}_{m}=Q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$

In this case, the charged particle is released from rest along the axis. The magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is also along the axis. Therefore, the velocity $\vec{v}$ (once the particle starts moving) and the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ are parallel to each other.

The magnitude of the magnetic force is the cross product of $Q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$ ,

$F_{m}=QvBsin\theta$

Since the angle $\theta$ between the velocity and the magnetic field is $0^{\circ}$ :

$F_{m}=QvBsin0^{\circ}$

The magnetic field exerts no force on the particle moving along the axis.

The solenoid is placed vertically. When the particle of mass $m$ is released, the only non-zero force acting on it is the force of gravity $(\vec{F}_{g})$ :

$\vec{F}_{g}=mg$

This force acts vertically downwards along the axis of the solenoid.

According to Newton's Second Law ( $F_{\text{net}}=ma$ ) :

$mg=ma$

$\Rightarrow a=g$

Since the magnetic force is zero the particle falls freely under gravity. Thus, its acceleration is exactly equal to g.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.question_text: 1 μC charge moving with velocity $\vec{v}=(\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k})$ m/s in the region of magnetic field $\vec{B}=(2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-5\hat{k})$ T. The magnitude of force acting on it is $\sqrt{\alpha} \times 10^{-6}$ N. The value of $\alpha$ is _______.
questions.question_html: 1 μC charge moving with velocity $\vec{v}=(\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k})$ m/s in the region of magnetic field $\vec{B}=(2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-5\hat{k})$ T. The magnitude of force acting on it is $\sqrt{\alpha} \times 10^{-6}$ N. The value of $\alpha$ is _______.
questions.explanation_text: The magnetic force acting on a charge $q$ moving with velocity $\vec{v}$ in a magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is given by : $\vec{F}=q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$ $\vec{F}=q|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ v_{x} & v_{y} & v_{z} \\ B_{x} & B_{y} & B_{z} \end{aligned}|$ $\vec{F}=1 \times 10^{-6}|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -2 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 & -5 \end{aligned}|$ Expanding the determinant: $\vec{F}=1 \times 10^{-6}(\hat{i}[(-2)(-5)-(3)(3)]-\hat{j}[(1)(-5)-(3)(2)]+\hat{k}[(1)(3)-(-2)(2)])$ $\vec{F}=1 \times 10^{-6}[\hat{i}(10-9)-\hat{j}(-5-6)+\hat{k}(3+4)]$ $\vec{F}=1 \times 10^{-6}[1\hat{i}+11\hat{j}+7\hat{k}]$ So, the magnitude $|\vec{F}|$ is: $|\vec{F}|=10^{-6}\sqrt{1^{2}+11^{2}+7^{2}}$ $|\vec{F}|=10^{-6}\sqrt{1+121+49}$ $|\vec{F}|=\sqrt{171} \times 10^{-6}N$ $\Rightarrow \sqrt{\alpha} \times 10^{-6}N=\sqrt{171} \times 10^{-6}N$ $\Rightarrow \alpha=171$ Therefore, the value of $\alpha$ is $171$ . Thus, the correct answer is $171$ .
questions.explanation_html:
The magnetic force acting on a charge $q$ moving with velocity $\vec{v}$ in a magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is given by :

$\vec{F}=q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$

$\vec{F}=q|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ v_{x} & v_{y} & v_{z} \\ B_{x} & B_{y} & B_{z} \end{aligned}|$

$\vec{F}=1 \times 10^{-6}|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -2 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 & -5 \end{aligned}|$

Expanding the determinant:

$\vec{F}=1 \times 10^{-6}(\hat{i}[(-2)(-5)-(3)(3)]-\hat{j}[(1)(-5)-(3)(2)]+\hat{k}[(1)(3)-(-2)(2)])$

$\vec{F}=1 \times 10^{-6}[\hat{i}(10-9)-\hat{j}(-5-6)+\hat{k}(3+4)]$

$\vec{F}=1 \times 10^{-6}[1\hat{i}+11\hat{j}+7\hat{k}]$

So, the magnitude $|\vec{F}|$ is:

$|\vec{F}|=10^{-6}\sqrt{1^{2}+11^{2}+7^{2}}$

$|\vec{F}|=10^{-6}\sqrt{1+121+49}$

$|\vec{F}|=\sqrt{171} \times 10^{-6}N$

$\Rightarrow \sqrt{\alpha} \times 10^{-6}N=\sqrt{171} \times 10^{-6}N$

$\Rightarrow \alpha=171$

Therefore, the value of $\alpha$ is $171$ . Thus, the correct answer is $171$ .

questions.question_text: A small cube of side 1 mm is placed at the centre of a circular loop of radius 10 cm carrying a current of 2 A . The magnetic energy stored inside the cube is $\alpha \times 10^{-14}J$ . The value of $\alpha$ is $____$ . $(\mu_{o}=4\pi \times 10^{-7}Tm/A,\pi=3.14)$
questions.question_html:
A small cube of side 1 mm is placed at the centre of a circular loop of radius 10 cm carrying a current of 2 A . The magnetic energy stored inside the cube is $\alpha \times 10^{-14}J$ . The value of $\alpha$ is $____$ .

$(\mu_{o}=4\pi \times 10^{-7}Tm/A,\pi=3.14)$
questions.explanation_text: The magnetic field produced at the center of a circular wire of radius $r$ carrying current $I$ is: $B=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2r}$ The electric current in the circular loop is $I=2A$ , the radius of the loop is $r=10cm=0.1m$ . $B=\frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 2}{2 \times 0.1}=4\pi \times 10^{-6}T$ Magnetic energy is stored in the space where a magnetic field exists. The energy per unit volume is: $u_{B}=\frac{B^{2}}{2\mu_{0}}$ For a very small volume V where the field B is approximately uniform: $U=u_{B} \times V=\frac{B^{2}}{2\mu_{0}} \times V$ The volume of the cube is, $V=(1mm)^{3}=(10^{-3}m)^{3}=10^{-9}m^{3}$ So, the total energy stored in the cube is, $U=\frac{(4\pi \times 10^{-6})^{2}}{2 \times 4\pi \times 10^{-7}} \times 10^{-9}$ $\Rightarrow$ $U=\frac{16\pi^{2} \times 10^{-12}}{8\pi \times 10^{-7}} \times 10^{-9}=2\pi \times 10^{-5} \times 10^{-9}$ $\Rightarrow$ $U=2 \times 3.14 \times 10^{-14}=6.28 \times 10^{-14}J=\alpha \times 10^{-14}J$ $\Rightarrow \alpha=6.28$ Therefore, the correct option is (A).
questions.explanation_html:
The magnetic field produced at the center of a circular wire of radius $r$ carrying current $I$ is:

$B=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2r}$

The electric current in the circular loop is $I=2A$ , the radius of the loop is $r=10cm=0.1m$ .

$B=\frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 2}{2 \times 0.1}=4\pi \times 10^{-6}T$

Magnetic energy is stored in the space where a magnetic field exists. The energy per unit volume is:

$u_{B}=\frac{B^{2}}{2\mu_{0}}$

For a very small volume V where the field B is approximately uniform:

$U=u_{B} \times V=\frac{B^{2}}{2\mu_{0}} \times V$

The volume of the cube is,

$V=(1mm)^{3}=(10^{-3}m)^{3}=10^{-9}m^{3}$

So, the total energy stored in the cube is,

$U=\frac{(4\pi \times 10^{-6})^{2}}{2 \times 4\pi \times 10^{-7}} \times 10^{-9}$

$\Rightarrow$ $U=\frac{16\pi^{2} \times 10^{-12}}{8\pi \times 10^{-7}} \times 10^{-9}=2\pi \times 10^{-5} \times 10^{-9}$

$\Rightarrow$ $U=2 \times 3.14 \times 10^{-14}=6.28 \times 10^{-14}J=\alpha \times 10^{-14}J$

$\Rightarrow \alpha=6.28$

Therefore, the correct option is (A).

questions.question_text: Two identical long current carrying wires are bent into the shapes shown in the following figures. If the magnitude of magnetic fields at the centres P and Q of a semicircular arc are $B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$ respectively, then the ratio $\frac{B_{1}}{B_{2}}$ is ______.
questions.question_html: Two identical long current carrying wires are bent into the shapes shown in the following figures. If the magnitude of magnetic fields at the centres P and Q of a semicircular arc are $B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$ respectively, then the ratio $\frac{B_{1}}{B_{2}}$ is ______.
questions.explanation_text: For semi-infinite straight wire the field at a distance $r$ from wire is $B=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}$ The field at the centre of a circular arc subtending angle $\phi$ is $B=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}\phi$ , where $\phi$ is in radians. For a semicircle, $\phi=\pi$ , so $B=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4r}$ . For system of current carrying wire (I), the direction of magnetic field using right hand rule is into the page due to semi-infinite wires and semi-circular wire. Field from two semi-infinite wires is $2 \times \frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r}$ Field from semicircle is $\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4r}$ As they act in the same direction, the net magnetic field is, $B_{1}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4r}+\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}(\pi+2)$ The system of current carrying wires (II) consists of two straight wire and one semi-circular wire. One of the straight wire is passing through the point Q, so the magnetic field due to the wire which passes through the same point where magnetic field is to be calculated is zero. So, the magnetic field due to semi-infinite wire is $\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}$ The magnetic field due to semi-circular wire is $\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4r}$ As they act in the same direction, the net magnetic field is, $B_{2}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}+\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4r}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}(\pi+1)$ Therefore, the ratio of magnetic fields is, $\frac{B_{1}}{B_{2}}=\frac{\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}(\pi+2)}{\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}(\pi+1)}$ The ratio of the magnetic fields is $\frac{2+\pi}{1+\pi}$ . Thus, the correct option is (A).
questions.explanation_html:
For semi-infinite straight wire the field at a distance $r$ from wire is

$B=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}$

The field at the centre of a circular arc subtending angle $\phi$ is $B=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}\phi$ , where $\phi$ is in radians.

For a semicircle, $\phi=\pi$ , so $B=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4r}$ .

For system of current carrying wire (I), the direction of magnetic field using right hand rule is into the page due to semi-infinite wires and semi-circular wire.

Field from two semi-infinite wires is $2 \times \frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r}$

Field from semicircle is $\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4r}$

As they act in the same direction, the net magnetic field is,

$B_{1}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4r}+\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}(\pi+2)$

The system of current carrying wires (II) consists of two straight wire and one semi-circular wire.

One of the straight wire is passing through the point Q, so the magnetic field due to the wire which passes through the same point where magnetic field is to be calculated is zero.

So, the magnetic field due to semi-infinite wire is $\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}$

The magnetic field due to semi-circular wire is $\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4r}$

As they act in the same direction, the net magnetic field is,

$B_{2}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}+\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4r}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}(\pi+1)$

Therefore, the ratio of magnetic fields is,

$\frac{B_{1}}{B_{2}}=\frac{\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}(\pi+2)}{\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}(\pi+1)}$

The ratio of the magnetic fields is $\frac{2+\pi}{1+\pi}$ . Thus, the correct option is (A).

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: Two identical circular loops $P$ and $Q$ each of radius $r$ are lying in parallel planes such that they have common axis. The current through $P$ and $Q$ are $I$ and $4I$ respectively in clockwise direction as seen from $O$ . The net magnetic field at $O$ is :
questions.question_html: Two identical circular loops $P$ and $Q$ each of radius $r$ are lying in parallel planes such that they have common axis. The current through $P$ and $Q$ are $I$ and $4I$ respectively in clockwise direction as seen from $O$ . The net magnetic field at $O$ is :
questions.explanation_text: The magnetic field (B) on the axis of a circular loop of radius $r$ at a distance $x$ from its center is given by : $B=\frac{\mu_{0}Ir^{2}}{2(r^{2}+x^{2})^{3/2}}$ The point O is at a distance $x=r$ from the center of both loops P and Q . For loop P : Current is $i=I$ . The magnetic field $B_{P}$ at O due to loop P is : $B_{P}=\frac{\mu_{0}Ir^{2}}{2(r^{2}+r^{2})^{3/2}}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\sqrt{2}r}$ Using the right-hand thumb rule, the current is clockwise as seen from O , so the field $B_{P}$ due to loop P points towards P. For loop Q : Current is $i=4I$ . The magnetic field $B_{Q}$ at O due to loop Q is: $B_{Q}=\frac{\mu_{0}(4I)r^{2}}{2(r^{2}+r^{2})^{3/2}}=\frac{4\mu_{0}I}{4\sqrt{2}r}$ Using the right-hand thumb rule, the current is clockwise as seen from O , so the field $B_{Q}$ due to loop Q points towards Q. The net magnetic field $(B_{net})$ at $O$ is the vector sum of these opposing fields. Since $B_{Q}>B_{P}$ , the net field will be in the direction of $B_{Q}$ (towards Q ): $B_{net}=B_{Q}-B_{P}=\frac{4\mu_{0}I}{4\sqrt{2}r}-\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\sqrt{2}r}=\frac{3\mu_{0}I}{4\sqrt{2}r}$ Therefore, the resulting magnetic field at the midpoint is $\frac{3\mu_{0}I}{4\sqrt{2}r}$ towards $Q$ . Hence, the correct option is (B).
questions.explanation_html:
The magnetic field (B) on the axis of a circular loop of radius $r$ at a distance $x$ from its center is given by :

$B=\frac{\mu_{0}Ir^{2}}{2(r^{2}+x^{2})^{3/2}}$

The point O is at a distance $x=r$ from the center of both loops P and Q .

For loop P :

Current is $i=I$ .

The magnetic field $B_{P}$ at O due to loop P is :

$B_{P}=\frac{\mu_{0}Ir^{2}}{2(r^{2}+r^{2})^{3/2}}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\sqrt{2}r}$

Using the right-hand thumb rule, the current is clockwise as seen from O , so the field $B_{P}$ due to loop P points towards P.

For loop Q :

Current is $i=4I$ .

The magnetic field $B_{Q}$ at O due to loop Q is:

$B_{Q}=\frac{\mu_{0}(4I)r^{2}}{2(r^{2}+r^{2})^{3/2}}=\frac{4\mu_{0}I}{4\sqrt{2}r}$

Using the right-hand thumb rule, the current is clockwise as seen from O , so the field $B_{Q}$ due to loop Q points towards Q.

The net magnetic field $(B_{net})$ at $O$ is the vector sum of these opposing fields. Since $B_{Q}>B_{P}$ , the net field will be in the direction of $B_{Q}$ (towards Q ):

$B_{net}=B_{Q}-B_{P}=\frac{4\mu_{0}I}{4\sqrt{2}r}-\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\sqrt{2}r}=\frac{3\mu_{0}I}{4\sqrt{2}r}$

Therefore, the resulting magnetic field at the midpoint is $\frac{3\mu_{0}I}{4\sqrt{2}r}$ towards $Q$ .

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: A particle of charge $q$ and mass $m$ is projected from origin with an initial velocity $\vec{v}=(\frac{v_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{x}+\frac{v_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{y})$ . There exists a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}=B_{0}\hat{z}$ and a space varying electric field $\vec{E}=E_{o}e^{-\lambda x}\hat{x}$ within the region $0⩽x⩽L$ . After travelling a distance such that $x$ -coordinate has changed from $x=0$ to $x=L$ , the change in the kinetic energy is $____$ .
questions.question_html: A particle of charge $q$ and mass $m$ is projected from origin with an initial velocity $\vec{v}=(\frac{v_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{x}+\frac{v_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{y})$ . There exists a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}=B_{0}\hat{z}$ and a space varying electric field $\vec{E}=E_{o}e^{-\lambda x}\hat{x}$ within the region $0⩽x⩽L$ . After travelling a distance such that $x$ -coordinate has changed from $x=0$ to $x=L$ , the change in the kinetic energy is $____$ .
questions.explanation_text: The magnetic force $\vec{F}_{m}$ acting on a charged particle is given by $\vec{F}_{m}=q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$ . So, the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity of the particle $(\vec{F}_{m}⟂\vec{v})$ . Since the force is perpendicular to the displacement at every instant, the work done by the magnetic field is always zero: $W_{m}=\int \vec{F}_{m} \cdot d\vec{r}=0$ The electric force $\vec{F}_{e}$ is given by $\vec{F}_{e}=q\vec{E}$ . The electric field in the region is given as $\vec{E}=E_{o}e^{-\lambda x}\hat{x}$ , the force is: $\vec{F}_{e}=qE_{o}e^{-\lambda x_{\hat{x}}}$ The work done by the electric field as the particle moves from $x=0$ to $x=L$ is : $W_{e}=\int_{0}^{L}\vec{F}_{e} \cdot d\vec{x}$ $\Rightarrow$ $W_{e}=\int_{0}^{L}qE_{o}e^{-\lambda x} \cdot dx$ $\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow W_{e}=eE_{0}\int_{0}^{L}e^{-\lambda x} \cdot dx \\ \Rightarrow W_{e}=eE_{0}[\frac{e^{-\lambda x}}{-\lambda}]_{0}^{L} \\ \Rightarrow W_{e}=-\frac{qE_{o}}{\lambda}[e^{-\lambda L}-e^{0}] \\ \Rightarrow W_{e}=-\frac{qE_{o}}{\lambda}[e^{-\lambda L}-1] \\ \Rightarrow W_{e}=\frac{qE_{o}}{\lambda}[1-e^{-\lambda L}] \end{aligned}$ Using work-energy theory, the total work done on particle is equal to total change in kinetic energy. $\begin{aligned} \Delta K=W_{\text{total}}=W_{m}+W_{e} \\ \Delta K=0+\frac{qE_{o}}{\lambda}[1-e^{-\lambda L}] \\ \Delta K=\frac{qE_{o}}{\lambda}[1-e^{-\lambda L}] \end{aligned}$ Therefore, the change in kinetic energy is $\frac{qE_{0}}{\lambda}[1-e^{-\lambda L}]$ . Thus, the correct option is (A).
questions.explanation_html:
The magnetic force $\vec{F}_{m}$ acting on a charged particle is given by $\vec{F}_{m}=q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$ .

So, the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity of the particle $(\vec{F}_{m}⟂\vec{v})$ .

Since the force is perpendicular to the displacement at every instant, the work done by the magnetic field is always zero:

$W_{m}=\int \vec{F}_{m} \cdot d\vec{r}=0$

The electric force $\vec{F}_{e}$ is given by $\vec{F}_{e}=q\vec{E}$ .

The electric field in the region is given as $\vec{E}=E_{o}e^{-\lambda x}\hat{x}$ , the force is:

$\vec{F}_{e}=qE_{o}e^{-\lambda x_{\hat{x}}}$

The work done by the electric field as the particle moves from $x=0$ to $x=L$ is :

$W_{e}=\int_{0}^{L}\vec{F}_{e} \cdot d\vec{x}$

$\Rightarrow$ $W_{e}=\int_{0}^{L}qE_{o}e^{-\lambda x} \cdot dx$

$\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow W_{e}=eE_{0}\int_{0}^{L}e^{-\lambda x} \cdot dx \\ \Rightarrow W_{e}=eE_{0}[\frac{e^{-\lambda x}}{-\lambda}]_{0}^{L} \\ \Rightarrow W_{e}=-\frac{qE_{o}}{\lambda}[e^{-\lambda L}-e^{0}] \\ \Rightarrow W_{e}=-\frac{qE_{o}}{\lambda}[e^{-\lambda L}-1] \\ \Rightarrow W_{e}=\frac{qE_{o}}{\lambda}[1-e^{-\lambda L}] \end{aligned}$

Using work-energy theory, the total work done on particle is equal to total change in kinetic energy.

$\begin{aligned} \Delta K=W_{\text{total}}=W_{m}+W_{e} \\ \Delta K=0+\frac{qE_{o}}{\lambda}[1-e^{-\lambda L}] \\ \Delta K=\frac{qE_{o}}{\lambda}[1-e^{-\lambda L}] \end{aligned}$

Therefore, the change in kinetic energy is $\frac{qE_{0}}{\lambda}[1-e^{-\lambda L}]$ .

Thus, the correct option is (A).

questions.question_text: A long cylindrical conductor with large cross section carries an electric current distributed uniformly over its cross-section. Magnetic field due to this current is: A. maximum at either ends of the conductor and minimum at the midpoint B. maximum at the axis of the conductor C. minimum at the surface of the conductor D. minimum at the axis of the conductor E. same at all points in the cross-section of the conductor Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.question_html:
A long cylindrical conductor with large cross section carries an electric current distributed uniformly over its cross-section. Magnetic field due to this current is:

A. maximum at either ends of the conductor and minimum at the midpoint

B. maximum at the axis of the conductor

C. minimum at the surface of the conductor

D. minimum at the axis of the conductor

E. same at all points in the cross-section of the conductor

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.label: A
options.html: B, C Only

options.label: C
options.html: A, D Only

questions.explanation_text: Consider a long, straight wire of radius R carrying a steady current I. Since the current distribution is uniform, the current density (J) is constant throughout the cross-section. The current density J is given by : $J=\frac{I}{\text{Total Area}}=\frac{I}{\pi R^{2}}$ Ampère's Law states that the line integral of the magnetic field B around a closed loop (Amperian loop) is equal to $\mu_{0}$ times the current enclosed ( $I_{enc}$ ) by that loop : $∮B \cdot dl=\mu_{0}I_{enc}$ To find the field inside, consider a circular Amperian loop of radius $r$ (where $r<R$ ) centered on the wire's axis. $∮Bdl=B∮dl=B(2\pi r)$ The current enclosed is, $I_{enc}=J \times (\text{Area of loop})=(\frac{I}{\pi R^{2}}) \times (\pi r^{2})$ $\Rightarrow$ $I_{enc}=\frac{Ir^{2}}{R^{2}}$ Using Ampère's Law : $B(2\pi r)=\mu_{0}(\frac{Ir^{2}}{R^{2}})$ $\Rightarrow$ $B=\frac{\mu_{0}Ir^{2}}{2\pi r^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $B=\frac{\mu_{0}Ir}{2\pi R^{2}}$ The magnetic field inside the wire increases linearly with the distance r from the center. $B∝r$ At the axis of the conductor ( $r=0$ ), the magnetic field $B$ becomes zero (minimum). Hence, statement $B$ is incorrect and statement D is correct. For a point outside the conductor $(r>R)$ : Since the Amperian loop (radius $r$ ) completely surrounds the entire cross-section of the cylinder (radius R), it encloses the total current I flowing through the conductor. $I_{enc}=I$ Using Ampère's Law equation : $B(2\pi r)=\mu_{0}I$ $\Rightarrow$ $B=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r}$ This shows that B is inversely proportional to $r(B∝\frac{1}{r})$ . The field is maximum at the surface ( $r=R$ ) and decreases when moving further away. Hence, statement C is incorrect. The field distribution depends on the distance from the axis, not the length/midpoint of the conductor. Hence, statement (A) is incorrect. Since, the field varies linearly inside and inversely outside; it is not uniform. Hence, option E is incorrect. Therefore, only statement D is correct. Hence, the correct option is (D).
questions.explanation_html:
Consider a long, straight wire of radius R carrying a steady current I. Since the current distribution is uniform, the current density (J) is constant throughout the cross-section.

The current density J is given by :

$J=\frac{I}{\text{Total Area}}=\frac{I}{\pi R^{2}}$

Ampère's Law states that the line integral of the magnetic field B around a closed loop (Amperian loop) is equal to $\mu_{0}$ times the current enclosed ( $I_{enc}$ ) by that loop :

$∮B \cdot dl=\mu_{0}I_{enc}$

To find the field inside, consider a circular Amperian loop of radius $r$ (where $r<R$ ) centered on the wire's axis.

$∮Bdl=B∮dl=B(2\pi r)$

The current enclosed is,

$I_{enc}=J \times (\text{Area of loop})=(\frac{I}{\pi R^{2}}) \times (\pi r^{2})$

$\Rightarrow$ $I_{enc}=\frac{Ir^{2}}{R^{2}}$

Using Ampère's Law :

$B(2\pi r)=\mu_{0}(\frac{Ir^{2}}{R^{2}})$

$\Rightarrow$ $B=\frac{\mu_{0}Ir^{2}}{2\pi r^{2}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $B=\frac{\mu_{0}Ir}{2\pi R^{2}}$

The magnetic field inside the wire increases linearly with the distance r from the center.

$B∝r$

At the axis of the conductor ( $r=0$ ), the magnetic field $B$ becomes zero (minimum). Hence, statement $B$ is incorrect and statement D is correct.

For a point outside the conductor $(r>R)$ :

Since the Amperian loop (radius $r$ ) completely surrounds the entire cross-section of the cylinder (radius R), it encloses the total current I flowing through the conductor.

$I_{enc}=I$

Using Ampère's Law equation :

$B(2\pi r)=\mu_{0}I$

$\Rightarrow$ $B=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r}$

This shows that B is inversely proportional to $r(B∝\frac{1}{r})$ .

The field is maximum at the surface ( $r=R$ ) and decreases when moving further away. Hence, statement C is incorrect.

The field distribution depends on the distance from the axis, not the length/midpoint of the conductor. Hence, statement (A) is incorrect.

Since, the field varies linearly inside and inversely outside; it is not uniform. Hence, option E is incorrect.

Therefore, only statement D is correct.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.question_text: The current passing through a conducting loop in the form of equilateral triangle of side $4\sqrt{3}cm$ is 2 A . The magnetic field at its centroid is $\alpha \times 10^{-5}T$ . The value of $\alpha$ is $____$ . (Given : $\mu_{o}=4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ SI units)
questions.question_html:
The current passing through a conducting loop in the form of equilateral triangle of side $4\sqrt{3}cm$ is 2 A . The magnetic field at its centroid is $\alpha \times 10^{-5}T$ . The value of $\alpha$ is $____$ .

(Given : $\mu_{o}=4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ SI units)
questions.explanation_text: Let L be the side of the equilateral triangle, where $L=4\sqrt{3}cm=4\sqrt{3} \times 10^{-2}m$ . The centroid $O$ is equidistant from all three sides. Let $r$ be the perpendicular distance from the centroid to any side. In an equilateral triangle : $tan60^{\circ}=\sqrt{3}=\frac{L/2}{r} \Rightarrow r=\frac{L}{2\sqrt{3}}$ Substituting the value of L : $r=\frac{4\sqrt{3} \times 10^{-2}}{2\sqrt{3}}=2 \times 10^{-2}m$ The magnetic field $B_{1}$ due to a straight wire of finite length at a distance $r$ is given by : $B_{1}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}(sin\theta_{1}+sin\theta_{2})$ Here, $\theta_{1}=\theta_{2}=60^{\circ}$ $B_{1}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}(sin60^{\circ}+sin60^{\circ})=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}(2sin60^{\circ})$ $\Rightarrow$ $B_{1}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}(2 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})=\frac{\mu_{0}I\sqrt{3}}{4\pi r}$ Since there are three sides and the current flows in a way that all three fields at the centroid point in the same direction, $B_{net}=3 \times B_{1}=\frac{3\sqrt{3}\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}$ Substituting the given values : 1. $\mu_{0}=4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ 2. $I=2A$ 3. $r=2 \times 10^{-2}m$ $B_{net}=\frac{3\sqrt{3} \times (4\pi \times 10^{-7}) \times 2}{4\pi \times (2 \times 10^{-2})}T$ $\Rightarrow$ $B_{net}=\frac{3\sqrt{3} \times 10^{-7} \times 2}{2 \times 10^{-2}}T$ $\Rightarrow$ $B_{net}=3\sqrt{3} \times 10^{-5}T=\alpha \times 10^{-5}T$ $\Rightarrow \alpha=3\sqrt{3}$
questions.explanation_html:
Let L be the side of the equilateral triangle, where $L=4\sqrt{3}cm=4\sqrt{3} \times 10^{-2}m$ .

The centroid $O$ is equidistant from all three sides. Let $r$ be the perpendicular distance from the centroid to any side.

In an equilateral triangle :

$tan60^{\circ}=\sqrt{3}=\frac{L/2}{r} \Rightarrow r=\frac{L}{2\sqrt{3}}$

Substituting the value of L :

$r=\frac{4\sqrt{3} \times 10^{-2}}{2\sqrt{3}}=2 \times 10^{-2}m$

The magnetic field $B_{1}$ due to a straight wire of finite length at a distance $r$ is given by :

$B_{1}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}(sin\theta_{1}+sin\theta_{2})$

Here, $\theta_{1}=\theta_{2}=60^{\circ}$

$B_{1}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}(sin60^{\circ}+sin60^{\circ})=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}(2sin60^{\circ})$

$\Rightarrow$ $B_{1}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}(2 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})=\frac{\mu_{0}I\sqrt{3}}{4\pi r}$

Since there are three sides and the current flows in a way that all three fields at the centroid point in the same direction,

$B_{net}=3 \times B_{1}=\frac{3\sqrt{3}\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}$

Substituting the given values :

  • 1. $\mu_{0}=4\pi \times 10^{-7}$

  • 2. $I=2A$

  • 3. $r=2 \times 10^{-2}m$

$B_{net}=\frac{3\sqrt{3} \times (4\pi \times 10^{-7}) \times 2}{4\pi \times (2 \times 10^{-2})}T$

$\Rightarrow$ $B_{net}=\frac{3\sqrt{3} \times 10^{-7} \times 2}{2 \times 10^{-2}}T$

$\Rightarrow$ $B_{net}=3\sqrt{3} \times 10^{-5}T=\alpha \times 10^{-5}T$

$\Rightarrow \alpha=3\sqrt{3}$

A bigger Amperian loop B encloses the whole circle where as a smaller Amperian loop A encloses a small segment. The difference between enclosed currents, $I_{A}-I_{B}$ , for the given Amperian loops is
questions.question_html: N equally spaced charges each of value q , are placed on a circle of radius R . The circle rotates about its axis with an angular velocity $\omega$ as shown in the figure. A bigger Amperian loop B encloses the whole circle where as a smaller Amperian loop A encloses a small segment. The difference between enclosed currents, $I_{A}-I_{B}$ , for the given Amperian loops is
questions.explanation_text: The total charge distributed on the circular ring is: $Q=Nq$ The time taken for one full rotation is: $T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}$ The rotating charges create an equivalent circular current given by: $I=\frac{Q}{T}=\frac{Nq}{\frac{2\pi}{\omega}}=\frac{Nq\omega}{2\pi}$ For Amperian loop $A$ , the circular current path passes directly through the area bounded by the loop. Therefore, the enclosed current is: $I_{A}=\frac{Nq\omega}{2\pi}$ For Amperian loop $B$ , the charges rotate entirely within the plane of the loop and do not cross or thread through the surface bounded by loop $B$ . Therefore, the current passing through loop $B$ is: $I_{B}=0$ Now, finding the difference between the two enclosed currents: $I_{A}-I_{B}=\frac{Nq\omega}{2\pi}-0=\frac{Nq\omega}{2\pi}$
questions.explanation_html:
The total charge distributed on the circular ring is:

$Q=Nq$

The time taken for one full rotation is:

$T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}$

The rotating charges create an equivalent circular current given by:

$I=\frac{Q}{T}=\frac{Nq}{\frac{2\pi}{\omega}}=\frac{Nq\omega}{2\pi}$

For Amperian loop $A$ , the circular current path passes directly through the area bounded by the loop. Therefore, the enclosed current is:

$I_{A}=\frac{Nq\omega}{2\pi}$

For Amperian loop $B$ , the charges rotate entirely within the plane of the loop and do not cross or thread through the surface bounded by loop $B$ . Therefore, the current passing through loop $B$ is:

$I_{B}=0$

Now, finding the difference between the two enclosed currents:

$I_{A}-I_{B}=\frac{Nq\omega}{2\pi}-0=\frac{Nq\omega}{2\pi}$

questions.question_text: A loop ABCDA , carrying current $I=12A$ , is placed in a plane, consists of two semi-circular segments of radius $R_{1}=6\pi m$ and $R_{2}=4\pi m$ . The magnitude of the resultant magnetic field at center O is $k \times 10^{-7}T$ . The value of k is_________. ( Given $\mu_{0}=4\pi \times 10^{-7}TmA^{-1}$ )
questions.question_html:
A loop ABCDA , carrying current $I=12A$ , is placed in a plane, consists of two semi-circular segments of radius $R_{1}=6\pi m$ and $R_{2}=4\pi m$ . The magnitude of the resultant magnetic field at center O is $k \times 10^{-7}T$ . The value of k is_________.

( Given $\mu_{0}=4\pi \times 10^{-7}TmA^{-1}$ )
questions.explanation_text: Magnetic Field from Semi-Circular Segments : The magnetic field at the center due to a semi-circular loop is given by: $B=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4R}$ Calculating $B_{R_{1}}$ and $B_{R_{2}}$ : For the semi-circle with radius $R_{1}$ : $B_{R_{1}}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4R_{1}}=\frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 12}{4 \times 6\pi}$ For the semi-circle with radius $R_{2}$ : $B_{R_{2}}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4R_{2}}=\frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 12}{4 \times 4\pi}$ Net Magnetic Field at the Center (O) : The total magnetic field $B_{0}$ at the center is the difference between these two fields (since they are in opposite directions): $B_{0}=|B_{R_{1}}-B_{R_{2}}|$ Calculate: $B_{0}=\frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 12}{4}(\frac{1}{4\pi}-\frac{1}{6\pi})$ $B_{0}=12\pi \times 10^{-7}(\frac{1}{12\pi})$ $B_{0}=1 \times 10^{-7}\text{T}$ Value of $k$ : Given that the magnitude of the resultant magnetic field is $k \times 10^{-7}\text{T}$ , we find $k=1$ . Thus, the value of $k$ is 1.
questions.explanation_html:
Magnetic Field from Semi-Circular Segments:

The magnetic field at the center due to a semi-circular loop is given by:

$B=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4R}$

Calculating $B_{R_{1}}$ and $B_{R_{2}}$ :

For the semi-circle with radius $R_{1}$ :

$B_{R_{1}}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4R_{1}}=\frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 12}{4 \times 6\pi}$

For the semi-circle with radius $R_{2}$ :

$B_{R_{2}}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4R_{2}}=\frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 12}{4 \times 4\pi}$

Net Magnetic Field at the Center (O):

The total magnetic field $B_{0}$ at the center is the difference between these two fields (since they are in opposite directions):

$B_{0}=|B_{R_{1}}-B_{R_{2}}|$

Calculate:

$B_{0}=\frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 12}{4}(\frac{1}{4\pi}-\frac{1}{6\pi})$

$B_{0}=12\pi \times 10^{-7}(\frac{1}{12\pi})$

$B_{0}=1 \times 10^{-7}\text{T}$

Value of $k$ :

Given that the magnitude of the resultant magnetic field is $k \times 10^{-7}\text{T}$ , we find $k=1$ .

Thus, the value of $k$ is 1.

questions.question_text: A current of 5 A exists in a square loop of side $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}m$ . Then the magnitude of the magnetic field $B$ at the centre of the square loop will be $p \times 10^{-6}T$ . where, value of p is ________ $[$ Take $\mu_{0}=4\pi \times 10^{-7}TmA^{-1}$ ].
questions.question_html: A current of 5 A exists in a square loop of side $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}m$ . Then the magnitude of the magnetic field $B$ at the centre of the square loop will be $p \times 10^{-6}T$ . where, value of p is ________ $[$ Take $\mu_{0}=4\pi \times 10^{-7}TmA^{-1}$ ].
questions.explanation_text: $B=\frac{2\sqrt{2}\mu_{0}I}{\pi L}$ For a square loop of side length $L=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\text{m},$ the perpendicular distance from the center to any side is $d=\frac{L}{2}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\text{m}.$ For a finite straight wire, the magnetic field at a point at distance $d$ from the wire is given by the Biot–Savart expression $B_{\text{side}}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi d}(sin\theta_{1}+sin\theta_{2})$ where $\theta_{1}$ and $\theta_{2}$ are the angles between the extended wire and the line joining the ends of the wire with the observation point. For one side of the square, by symmetry, the midpoint of the side and the center of the square give $tan\theta=\frac{L/2}{L/2}=1 \Rightarrow \theta=45^{\circ}.$ Thus, $sin\theta_{1}=sin\theta_{2}=sin45^{\circ}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.$ Then the field due to one side is $B_{\text{side}}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi(\frac{L}{2})}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi(\frac{L}{2})}(\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}})=\frac{\mu_{0}I\sqrt{2}}{2\pi L}.$ Since there are 4 sides with contributions that add vectorially in the same direction at the center, the total magnetic field is $B=4 \cdot B_{\text{side}}=\frac{4\mu_{0}I\sqrt{2}}{2\pi L}=\frac{2\sqrt{2}\mu_{0}I}{\pi L}.$ Substitute $L=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},$ to obtain $B=\frac{2\sqrt{2}\mu_{0}I}{\pi(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})}=\frac{2\sqrt{2}\mu_{0}I\sqrt{2}}{\pi}=\frac{4\mu_{0}I}{\pi}.$ Using the provided values $I=5\text{A}\text{and}\mu_{0}=4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{T}\text{m/A},$ the magnetic field becomes $B=\frac{4 \times (4\pi \times 10^{-7}) \times 5}{\pi}=\frac{80\pi \times 10^{-7}}{\pi}=80 \times 10^{-7}\text{T}=8 \times 10^{-6}\text{T}.$ Thus, the value of $p$ is $p=8.$
questions.explanation_html:
$B=\frac{2\sqrt{2}\mu_{0}I}{\pi L}$

For a square loop of side length

$L=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\text{m},$

the perpendicular distance from the center to any side is

$d=\frac{L}{2}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\text{m}.$

For a finite straight wire, the magnetic field at a point at distance $d$ from the wire is given by the Biot–Savart expression

$B_{\text{side}}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi d}(sin\theta_{1}+sin\theta_{2})$

where $\theta_{1}$ and $\theta_{2}$ are the angles between the extended wire and the line joining the ends of the wire with the observation point. For one side of the square, by symmetry, the midpoint of the side and the center of the square give

$tan\theta=\frac{L/2}{L/2}=1 \Rightarrow \theta=45^{\circ}.$

Thus,

$sin\theta_{1}=sin\theta_{2}=sin45^{\circ}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.$

Then the field due to one side is

$B_{\text{side}}=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi(\frac{L}{2})}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi(\frac{L}{2})}(\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}})=\frac{\mu_{0}I\sqrt{2}}{2\pi L}.$

Since there are 4 sides with contributions that add vectorially in the same direction at the center, the total magnetic field is

$B=4 \cdot B_{\text{side}}=\frac{4\mu_{0}I\sqrt{2}}{2\pi L}=\frac{2\sqrt{2}\mu_{0}I}{\pi L}.$

Substitute

$L=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},$

to obtain

$B=\frac{2\sqrt{2}\mu_{0}I}{\pi(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})}=\frac{2\sqrt{2}\mu_{0}I\sqrt{2}}{\pi}=\frac{4\mu_{0}I}{\pi}.$

Using the provided values

$I=5\text{A}\text{and}\mu_{0}=4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{T}\text{m/A},$

the magnetic field becomes

$B=\frac{4 \times (4\pi \times 10^{-7}) \times 5}{\pi}=\frac{80\pi \times 10^{-7}}{\pi}=80 \times 10^{-7}\text{T}=8 \times 10^{-6}\text{T}.$

Thus, the value of $p$ is

$p=8.$

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
questions.question_html:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as $AssertionA$ and the other is labelled as Reason $R$

Assertion A : If Oxygen ion $(O^{-2})$ and Hydrogen ion $(H^{+})$ enter normal to the magnetic field with equal momentum, then the path of $O^{-2}$ ion has a smaller curvature than that of $H^{+}$ .

Reason R : A proton with same linear momentum as an electron will form a path of smaller radius of curvature on entering a uniform magnetic field perpendicularly.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below

options.label: A
options.text: Both $A$ and $R$ are true but $R$ is NOT the correct explanation of $A$
options.html: Both $A$ and $R$ are true but $R$ is NOT the correct explanation of $A$

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.html: Both $A$ and $R$ are true and $R$ is the correct explanation of $A$

questions.explanation_text: The explanation involves analyzing the motion of charged particles in a magnetic field using the concept of radius of curvature. When a charged particle moves perpendicularly to a magnetic field, the radius of curvature $r$ of its path is given by: $r=\frac{mv}{qB}=\frac{p}{qB}$ Where: $m$ is the mass of the particle. $v$ is the velocity. $q$ is the charge. $B$ is the magnetic field strength. $p$ is the momentum of the particle. From this formula, we can see that the radius of curvature $r$ is directly proportional to the momentum $p$ and inversely proportional to the charge $q$ . In the given scenario: The Oxygen ion $O^{-2}$ and the Hydrogen ion $H^{+}$ both enter the magnetic field with equal momentum. Since $O^{-2}$ has a charge of $-2e$ and $H^{+}$ has a charge of $+e$ , and given that $r∝\frac{1}{q}$ , the path of $O^{-2}$ will indeed have a smaller radius of curvature compared to that of $H^{+}$ . Therefore, the Assertion $A$ is true. The Reason $R$ states that a proton and an electron with the same linear momentum will form paths of different radii upon entering a magnetic field, with the proton having a smaller radius of curvature. This reasoning is based on the same principle, since the mass and charge of the electron and proton are different. However, this explanation does not directly justify the assertion about Oxygen and Hydrogen ions, so Reason $R$ is false in the context of explaining Assertion $A$ . Thus, the correct conclusion is that $A$ is true, but $R$ is false.

The explanation involves analyzing the motion of charged particles in a magnetic field using the concept of radius of curvature. When a charged particle moves perpendicularly to a magnetic field, the radius of curvature $r$ of its path is given by:

$r=\frac{mv}{qB}=\frac{p}{qB}$

Where:

$m$ is the mass of the particle.

$v$ is the velocity.

$q$ is the charge.

$B$ is the magnetic field strength.

$p$ is the momentum of the particle.

From this formula, we can see that the radius of curvature $r$ is directly proportional to the momentum $p$ and inversely proportional to the charge $q$ .

In the given scenario:

The Oxygen ion $O^{-2}$ and the Hydrogen ion $H^{+}$ both enter the magnetic field with equal momentum.

Since $O^{-2}$ has a charge of $-2e$ and $H^{+}$ has a charge of $+e$ , and given that $r∝\frac{1}{q}$ , the path of $O^{-2}$ will indeed have a smaller radius of curvature compared to that of $H^{+}$ .

Therefore, the Assertion $A$ is true.

The Reason $R$ states that a proton and an electron with the same linear momentum will form paths of different radii upon entering a magnetic field, with the proton having a smaller radius of curvature. This reasoning is based on the same principle, since the mass and charge of the electron and proton are different. However, this explanation does not directly justify the assertion about Oxygen and Hydrogen ions, so Reason $R$ is false in the context of explaining Assertion $A$ . Thus, the correct conclusion is that $A$ is true, but $R$ is false.

The symbol $\times$ indicates the cross product, meaning the force is perpendicular to both the velocity and magnetic field vectors. Given this, for the force $\bar{F}$ to be zero: The velocity $\bar{v}$ and the magnetic field $\bar{B}$ must be parallel (or anti-parallel). This condition will result in the angle $\theta=0^{\circ}$ or $180^{\circ}$ . Under these circumstances, the electron will not experience any magnetic force and will continue to move in a straight line with constant velocity, as the cross product becomes zero. Therefore, the reason (R) is indeed a valid explanation: the magnetic field being along the direction of the electron's velocity means no perpendicular force is applied to change its path.

questions.explanation_text: To calculate the magnetic force on a wire, we use the formula: $F=I\ell B$ Where: $I$ is the current in the wire (in amperes), $\ell$ is the length of the wire (in meters), $B$ is the magnetic field strength (in teslas). Given that: The current $I$ is 8 A, The length of the wire $\ell$ is 4.0 cm, which is 0.04 m (since 1 cm = 0.01 m), The magnetic field strength $B$ is 0.15 T, Substituting these values into the formula gives: $F=8 \times 0.04 \times 0.15$ Calculating this: $F=0.048N$ To convert this to millinewtons (mN), recall that $1N=1000mN$ . Therefore: $F=48mN$ Thus, the magnetic force on the wire is 48 mN.

questions.question_text: A proton is moving undeflected in a region of crossed electric and magnetic fields at a constant speed of $2 \times 10^{5}ms^{-1}$ . When the electric field is switched off, the proton moves along a circular path of radius 2 cm . The magnitude of electric field is $x \times 10^{4}N/C$ . The value of $x$ is _________. Take the mass of the proton $=1.6 \times 10^{-27}kg$ .
questions.question_html: A proton is moving undeflected in a region of crossed electric and magnetic fields at a constant speed of $2 \times 10^{5}ms^{-1}$ . When the electric field is switched off, the proton moves along a circular path of radius 2 cm . The magnitude of electric field is $x \times 10^{4}N/C$ . The value of $x$ is _________. Take the mass of the proton $=1.6 \times 10^{-27}kg$ .
questions.explanation_text: Let's break down the problem step by step: When the proton moves undeflected in crossed electric and magnetic fields, the electric and magnetic forces balance each other. That is, $qE=qvB,$ which simplifies to $E=vB.$ After the electric field is switched off, the proton moves in a circular path under the action of the magnetic force. The magnetic force provides the required centripetal force: $qvB=\frac{mv^{2}}{r}.$ Solving for the magnetic field $B$ , we get: $B=\frac{mv}{qr}.$ Now substitute this expression for $B$ back into the equilibrium condition: $E=vB=v(\frac{mv}{qr})=\frac{mv^{2}}{qr}.$ Plug in the given values: Proton mass, $m=1.6 \times 10^{-27}\text{kg}$ Speed, $v=2 \times 10^{5}\text{m/s}$ Radius, $r=2\text{cm}=0.02\text{m}$ Proton charge, $q=1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{C}$ Thus, $E=\frac{(1.6 \times 10^{-27}\text{kg})(2 \times 10^{5}\text{m/s})^{2}}{(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{C})(0.02\text{m})}.$ Calculate the numerator: $(2 \times 10^{5})^{2}=4 \times 10^{10},$ So, $(1.6 \times 10^{-27}) \times (4 \times 10^{10})=6.4 \times 10^{-17}.$ Calculate the denominator: $(1.6 \times 10^{-19}) \times (0.02)=3.2 \times 10^{-21}.$ Now compute the electric field: $E=\frac{6.4 \times 10^{-17}}{3.2 \times 10^{-21}}=2 \times 10^{4}\text{N/C}.$ The problem states that the magnitude of the electric field is $x \times 10^{4}\text{N/C}.$ Since we found $E=2 \times 10^{4}\text{N/C},$ it follows that $x=2.$

When the proton moves undeflected in crossed electric and magnetic fields, the electric and magnetic forces balance each other. That is,

which simplifies to

$E=vB.$

After the electric field is switched off, the proton moves in a circular path under the action of the magnetic force. The magnetic force provides the required centripetal force:

$qvB=\frac{mv^{2}}{r}.$

Solving for the magnetic field $B$ , we get:

$B=\frac{mv}{qr}.$

Now substitute this expression for $B$ back into the equilibrium condition:

$E=vB=v(\frac{mv}{qr})=\frac{mv^{2}}{qr}.$

Plug in the given values:

Proton mass, $m=1.6 \times 10^{-27}\text{kg}$

Speed, $v=2 \times 10^{5}\text{m/s}$

Radius, $r=2\text{cm}=0.02\text{m}$

Proton charge, $q=1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{C}$

Thus,

$E=\frac{(1.6 \times 10^{-27}\text{kg})(2 \times 10^{5}\text{m/s})^{2}}{(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{C})(0.02\text{m})}.$

Calculate the numerator:

$(2 \times 10^{5})^{2}=4 \times 10^{10},$

So, $(1.6 \times 10^{-27}) \times (4 \times 10^{10})=6.4 \times 10^{-17}.$

$(1.6 \times 10^{-19}) \times (0.02)=3.2 \times 10^{-21}.$

The problem states that the magnitude of the electric field is $x \times 10^{4}\text{N/C}.$ Since we found

$E=2 \times 10^{4}\text{N/C},$

it follows that

$x=2.$

questions.question_html:
In a moving coil galvanometer, two moving coils $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ have the following particulars :

$\begin{aligned} & R_{1}=5\Omega,N_{1}=15,A_{1}=3.6 \times 10^{-3}m^{2},B_{1}=0.25T \\ & R_{2}=7\Omega,N_{2}=21,A_{2}=1.8 \times 10^{-3}m^{2},B_{2}=0.50T \end{aligned}$

Assuming that torsional constant of the springs are same for both coils, what will be the ratio of voltage sensitivity of $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ ?
questions.explanation_text: In a moving coil galvanometer, the voltage sensitivity is given by the formula: $\text{Voltage sensitivity}=\frac{\theta}{V}=\frac{N \cdot A \cdot B}{c \cdot R}$ Here, $\theta$ is the deflection angle, $V$ is the voltage, $N$ is the number of turns, $A$ is the coil area, $B$ is the magnetic field, $c$ is the torsional constant of the spring, and $R$ is the resistance of the coil. For the two moving coils $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ , we want to determine the ratio of their voltage sensitivities. Given that the torsional constant $c$ is the same for both coils, we can express the ratio as: $\text{Ratio of voltage sensitivities}=(\frac{N_{1} \cdot A_{1} \cdot B_{1}}{N_{2} \cdot A_{2} \cdot B_{2}}) \cdot \frac{R_{2}}{R_{1}}$ Plugging in the given values: $N_{1}=15$ $A_{1}=3.6 \times 10^{-3}\text{m}^{2}$ $B_{1}=0.25\text{T}$ $R_{1}=5\Omega$ $N_{2}=21$ $A_{2}=1.8 \times 10^{-3}\text{m}^{2}$ $B_{2}=0.50\text{T}$ $R_{2}=7\Omega$ We calculate: $\text{Ratio}=(\frac{15 \times 3.6 \times 0.25}{21 \times 1.8 \times 0.5}) \times \frac{7}{5}=\frac{1}{1}$ Thus, the ratio of the voltage sensitivities of $M_{1}$ to $M_{2}$ is 1:1.

2. The magnetic energy stored in the solenoid is :
questions.question_html: A solenoid having area A and length ' $l$ ' is filled with a material having relative permeability 2. The magnetic energy stored in the solenoid is :
questions.explanation_text: To determine the magnetic energy stored in a solenoid filled with a material of relative permeability 2, we start with the expression for energy density in a magnetic field: $\frac{U}{V}=\frac{B^{2}}{2\mu_{r}\mu_{0}}$ Given that the relative permeability $\mu_{r}$ is 2, this becomes: $\frac{U}{V}=\frac{B^{2}}{2 \times 2\mu_{0}}=\frac{B^{2}}{4\mu_{0}}$ The energy $U$ stored in the solenoid can be expressed as: $U=\frac{B^{2}}{4\mu_{0}} \times V$ Here, $V$ is the volume of the solenoid, calculated as $A \times \ell$ (where $A$ is the cross-sectional area and $\ell$ is the length). Therefore, substituting for $V$ , we get: $U=\frac{B^{2}}{4\mu_{0}} \times A\ell$ This formula gives us the magnetic energy stored in the solenoid.
questions.explanation_html:
To determine the magnetic energy stored in a solenoid filled with a material of relative permeability 2, we start with the expression for energy density in a magnetic field:

$\frac{U}{V}=\frac{B^{2}}{2\mu_{r}\mu_{0}}$

Given that the relative permeability $\mu_{r}$ is 2, this becomes:

$\frac{U}{V}=\frac{B^{2}}{2 \times 2\mu_{0}}=\frac{B^{2}}{4\mu_{0}}$

The energy $U$ stored in the solenoid can be expressed as:

$U=\frac{B^{2}}{4\mu_{0}} \times V$

Here, $V$ is the volume of the solenoid, calculated as $A \times \ell$ (where $A$ is the cross-sectional area and $\ell$ is the length). Therefore, substituting for $V$ , we get:

$U=\frac{B^{2}}{4\mu_{0}} \times A\ell$

This formula gives us the magnetic energy stored in the solenoid.
